title: Supporting anxious & nervous patients
blurb: Spot the signs of dental anxiety, build trust with tell-show-do, distraction and stop signals, and know when sedation is an option.
question: A new adult patient arrives late, grips the armrests and tells you she 'hasn't been to a dentist in ten years because of a bad experience'. The dentist is running a few minutes behind. What can you do to support her, and what should you tell the dentist?

teach.body: Dental anxiety is very common, and for some people it becomes a phobia so strong that they avoid the dentist until they are in pain. Avoidance lets disease get worse, so when they finally attend they need more invasive treatment, which feeds the fear. Your job is not to diagnose or decide treatment. It is to notice anxiety, listen, reassure, communicate clearly and make sure the dentist knows, so the team can plan care together.

teach.centre:
Break it with
trust and
prevention
teach.caption: Every calm, predictable visit weakens the cycle. Regular preventive care means less invasive treatment, so there is less to fear.

rows.label: Sweating, pale skin, fast shallow breathing
Gripping the armrests, tense shoulders, fidgeting
Cancelling, arriving late, putting off treatment
Talking fast, joking nervously, or saying very little
Crying, clinging to a parent, refusing to open

teach.note: Some practices use a short questionnaire such as the Modified Dental Anxiety Scale (MDAS) so the patient can rate their own fear.

teach.body: If a patient starts to talk about a bad experience, invite them to explain and listen calmly. Acknowledge how hard it sounds and ask what would help today. Your non-verbal communication matters as much as your words: a calm posture, an attentive expression, sitting at their eye level and a steady voice all lower tension. Avoid false promises such as 'this won't hurt at all'. If they say they might leave, acknowledge the feeling and tell the dentist straight away.

steps.label: Tell
steps.sub: Explain what will happen in simple, age-appropriate words

steps.label: Show
steps.sub: Demonstrate safely, e.g. air from the 3-in-1 on their hand

steps.label: Do
steps.sub: Carry it out exactly as described, with no surprises

steps.label: Praise
steps.sub: Reward cooperation to build confidence for next time

teach.caption: Tell-show-do works because it removes the unknown. It is used most with children but helps nervous adults too.

head: Technique
What it looks like
rows: Agree a raised hand before starting; always honour it
Music, a ceiling screen, a stress ball, counting
Prepare instruments and syringes out of view
Early slots and short waits leave less time to worry
Explain each step and agree pauses in advance

teach.text: When a patient uses the agreed stop signal, the team stops. Carrying on 'just to finish this bit' destroys trust, and a patient can withdraw consent at any point during treatment.

teach.h: When behavioural support is not enough
teach.caption: The dentist assesses and decides on sedation. General anaesthesia is only given in a hospital setting. Some patients are referred for psychological therapy such as CBT. Sedation nursing is an additional skill needing extra training.

items: Anxiety shows physically, in body language, behaviour and speech: notice it and tell the dentist.
Listen to past experiences, acknowledge them and ask what would help.
Tell-show-do, distraction, kind language and instruments out of view all reduce fear.
Agree a stop signal before starting and always honour it.
For severe anxiety the dentist may consider conscious sedation, referral or GA in hospital.

summary: You can now recognise the signs of dental anxiety, respond to a nervous patient by listening and reassuring, use tell-show-do, distraction and a stop signal, keep alarming instruments out of view, and explain when the dentist may consider conscious sedation or referral.

A.q: During her assessment, a patient mentions a past extraction 'went really badly' and then goes quiet. What should you do first?
options: Change the subject to keep her calm
Promise nothing will go wrong today
Invite her to talk about it and listen
Note it down and carry on setting up quietly
A.why: Inviting her to explain and listening calmly shows you take her fear seriously and helps the team understand what to avoid.

whyNot.0: Changing the subject dismisses her fear and you lose useful information.
whyNot.1: A promise you cannot guarantee breaks trust if anything is uncomfortable.
whyNot.3: Carrying on without responding ignores a clear sign of anxiety.

A.q: A patient agreed to raise his hand if he needs a break. Halfway through a filling, he raises it. What should happen?
options: The dentist stops as agreed and checks in
The dentist finishes the step, then stops
The nurse gently lowers his hand again
The team carries on unless he looks upset
A.why: An agreed stop signal must always be honoured straight away. That reliability is what makes the patient feel in control.

whyNot.1: Finishing first breaks the agreement and teaches him the signal does not work.
whyNot.2: Lowering his hand ignores his request and could amount to treating without consent.
whyNot.3: The signal itself is the request to stop; he does not have to look upset as well.

A.q: Which sequence correctly describes the tell-show-do technique?
options: Show the item, use it, then explain it
Do the procedure, then explain it after
Tell the parent, show the child, then do it
Explain it, demonstrate it, then do it
A.why: Tell-show-do means explaining in simple words, demonstrating safely, then doing exactly what was described.

whyNot.0: Showing before explaining puts the steps in the wrong order and can startle the patient.
whyNot.1: Explaining afterwards gives no chance to prepare and removes any sense of control.
whyNot.2: The explanation and demonstration are for the patient, including a child, not just the parent.

B.q: While you prepare the surgery, which action is most likely to increase an anxious patient's fear?
options: Talking them through what you are doing
Laying out forceps where they can see
Playing quiet music in the background
Sitting at their eye level to chat
B.why: Seeing instruments such as forceps or syringes is a common trigger. Prepare them out of the patient's line of sight.

whyNot.0: A calm explanation reduces the unknown and usually lowers anxiety.
whyNot.2: Music is a recognised distraction technique that can help nervous patients relax.
whyNot.3: Eye-level conversation feels less intimidating and builds rapport.

B.q: Just before the local anaesthetic, a patient says they are terrified of needles. What is the best response?
options: Say it will be over in a few seconds
Ask the dentist to inject before they tense
Tell the dentist and talk through options
Suggest they rebook when they feel braver
B.why: The operator needs to know so they can pause, reassure and discuss options with the patient, such as topical anaesthetic or a different approach.

whyNot.0: Brushing off the fear does not address it and may stop them speaking up again.
whyNot.1: Rushing the injection without the patient's agreement ignores their concern and their consent.
whyNot.3: Sending them away without discussing support could leave them avoiding care.

B.q: Which of these is NOT usually a sign of dental anxiety?
options: Repeatedly cancelling appointments
Gripping the armrests tightly
Talking fast and joking nervously
Slow, relaxed breathing
B.why: Slow, relaxed breathing suggests the patient is calm. Anxiety tends to cause fast, shallow breathing.

whyNot.0: Cancelling and putting off visits is a classic avoidance behaviour.
whyNot.1: White-knuckle gripping is a common body-language sign of fear.
whyNot.2: Rapid speech and nervous jokes often mask anxiety.

C.q: A patient in reception becomes agitated and says he might just go home. What should you do?
options: Remind him that missed visits are charged
Acknowledge how he feels and tell the dentist
Leave him alone for a while so he can calm down
Tell him there is nothing to worry about
C.why: Acknowledging his feelings shows empathy, and telling the dentist promptly lets the team adapt the visit before he leaves.

whyNot.0: Mentioning charges adds pressure and does nothing for his anxiety.
whyNot.2: Leaving him alone risks him walking out and avoiding care.
whyNot.3: Dismissing his fear can make him feel unheard.

C.q: A patient with severe dental phobia cannot tolerate treatment despite behavioural support. What might the dentist discuss?
options: Removing the stop signal so work continues
Asking the nurse to hold the patient still
Conscious sedation, such as IV midazolam
Working faster and explaining less
C.why: Conscious sedation, such as IV midazolam or inhalation sedation, can help when behavioural techniques are not enough. The patient stays awake and able to respond.

whyNot.0: The stop signal protects the patient's control and consent; removing it would worsen fear.
whyNot.1: Restraining an adult patient is not an acceptable way to manage anxiety.
whyNot.3: Less explanation increases the unknown, which drives anxiety up.

C.q: Which phrase is the best choice for a nervous patient about to have local anaesthetic?
options: 'This injection might hurt a little'
'Don't worry, this won't hurt at all'
'Try not to think about the needle'
'We're going to make the tooth numb'
C.why: Positive, non-threatening language describes what will happen without trigger words or false promises.

whyNot.0: Mentioning hurt primes the patient to expect pain.
whyNot.1: A false promise breaks trust if they feel any discomfort.
whyNot.2: Naming the needle draws attention to the very thing they fear.

reteach.title: Think of it like a first flight
reteach.question: Imagine a nervous flyer. What does good cabin crew do to help them, and how does that match your role in the surgery?

blocks.body: Good cabin crew explain what each noise means before it happens, keep calm faces, check in often and tell the nervous flyer how to call for help. That is exactly your job chairside. Explain each step before it happens (tell-show-do). Keep your face and voice calm. Agree how the patient can call a pause (the stop signal) and make sure it works. And tell the 'captain', the dentist, so the plan can change if needed.

steps.label: Notice
steps.sub: Spot the signs early, even in reception

steps.label: Listen
steps.sub: Invite them to explain; acknowledge it

steps.label: Tell the dentist
steps.sub: So the team can plan together

blocks.text: Reassurance is not the same as promising. 'We'll stop whenever you raise your hand' is a promise you can keep. 'It won't hurt' is not.

explain.body: Anxiety shows physically (sweating, pallor, fast breathing), in body language (gripping, tension), in behaviour (cancelling, arriving late) and in speech (talking fast, nervous jokes, or silence). Children may cry, cling or refuse to open.

test.q: Which observation most suggests a patient is anxious?
options: They ask about whitening options
They have cancelled three times
They arrive ten minutes early
They bring an updated medical history
test.why: Repeated cancellations are a typical avoidance behaviour linked to dental anxiety.

whyNot.0: Asking about cosmetic treatment shows interest, not fear.
whyNot.2: Arriving early is not a recognised sign of anxiety on its own.
whyNot.3: Bringing a medical history is good preparation, not a sign of fear.

explain.body: Invite the patient to explain past experiences and listen without interrupting. Acknowledge their feelings and ask what would help. Use a calm posture and attentive expression, and tell the dentist about any fears they share.

test.q: A tearful patient describes a painful past filling. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Tell her that was a different dentist
Explain modern fillings never hurt
Ask her to wait until she has stopped crying
Acknowledge it and ask what would help today
test.why: Acknowledging her experience and asking what would help shows empathy and gives her some control.

whyNot.0: This dismisses her feelings rather than addressing them.
whyNot.1: It is a false promise and minimises her experience.
whyNot.2: Asking her to wait ignores her distress instead of supporting her.

explain.body: Tell-show-do removes the unknown. Distraction (music, screens, stress balls) shifts attention. Kind language avoids trigger words. Instruments stay out of sight. A stop signal, agreed before starting and always honoured, gives the patient control.

letters.sub: Agree a stop signal and pauses
Instruments out of view, kind words

test.q: When should a stop signal be agreed with an anxious patient?
options: Before treatment starts
Only once they become upset
After the first injection
Only for child patients
test.why: Agreeing the signal before starting means the patient knows from the outset that they can pause treatment.

whyNot.1: Waiting until they are upset loses the reassurance the signal gives from the start.
whyNot.2: The injection is often the most feared part, so the signal is needed before it.
whyNot.3: Stop signals help anxious adults as much as children.

explain.body: For severe anxiety or phobia, the dentist may consider conscious sedation: inhalation sedation (nitrous oxide and oxygen) or IV sedation (usually midazolam). The patient stays awake and can respond. General anaesthesia is only given in hospital. Nurses need extra training to assist with sedation.

children.label: Dentist considers
children.sub: Sedation, GA in hospital, CBT referral

test.q: What is the key feature of conscious sedation?
options: The patient is fully asleep throughout
It is only allowed in hospitals
The patient stays awake and can respond
Written consent is not needed beforehand
test.why: In conscious sedation the patient is relaxed but remains conscious and able to respond to verbal contact.

whyNot.0: Being fully unconscious describes general anaesthesia, not conscious sedation.
whyNot.1: Conscious sedation is provided in suitably equipped dental practices; GA is hospital-only.
whyNot.3: Valid consent is always needed before sedation, and it should be in writing.
